reason: A nectary disc can be prominent or raised. The examples fit.
Colour of the stigma lobes. The examples are correct colour statements.
A seed can be concave-convex. But 'planoconvex' is a different shape and was wrongly mapped to this term. A rule would need to send plano-convex to its own term.
'Subsessile' on a pedicel really means a very short pedicel, not an attachment type. A rule would need to map subsessile and sessile on a stalk to length or absence.
Veins are annotated as vascular bundles. Branched and unbranched veins are meaningful.
A leaf blade can be arched. Some examples describe veins or the base, which is a part mix-up but not a wrong reading of the term.
Stems can be flexible or flaccid.
Ovaries are often hispid.
Trichomes can be filiform, which means thread-like.
Stems such as blackberry canes can be biennial. The examples are correct.
The examples are anther or pollen-sac sizes written as length by width. The androecium as a whole has no single width, so this is the wrong part.
Lodicules can be equal or unequal in size. The examples fit.
A petiole can be concave-convex in cross-section. The examples are correct.
A pedicel can be twisted.
A pinna or pinnule base can be decurrent. The examples are correct.
Leaf lobes can be glandular.
A peduncle or scape is measured by length. 'Tall' for a scape should be mapped to length, not to height.
Ovaries or ovary apices can be ciliate.
The sporangium base or neck has a length. The examples are correct.
A scale leaf can be long. Some examples describe other parts, but the pair itself is fine.
Filaments can be strap-shaped or ligulate.
Seeds can be scrobiculate (pitted). But the examples mention venation and surfaces, which are leaf statements. A rule would need to check that the bearer really is the seed.
Lateral veins can be branched or unbranched.
Flower heads can be globose or subglobose.
The number of viscidia is a count, which fits amount.
Presence of an involucel. The examples are about its position, but they still show it is present.
Leaves or their mesophyll can be dorsiventral.
Stipules can be strap-shaped (lorate).
Leaflets can be fan-shaped (flabellate).
Peduncles can be lanate (woolly).
Branches can be filiform.
Lobes can be ascending.
Capsules can be winged.
Bracts can be translucent.
A leaf blade can be aromatic.
Trichomes can be dendritic (branched like a tree).
The groove belongs to the petiole, not to its epidermis. The 'adaxial' in the text was read as the epidermis. It should be petiole + grooved, with the position kept separate.
Surface texture, such as scabrid or barbellate, is meaningful for this part.
An apex can be dilated or expanded.
Capsules can be short. Some examples compare with tepals or describe the neck, but the pair is meaningful.
Lobes can be reflexed or deflexed.
PATO_0000001 is the root 'quality' term and is too generic. The examples are shapes and positions that have their own terms.
Veins can be dense or lax.
'Structure' is too generic. The examples (articulate, adnate) are attachment or joining states and need their own terms.
Lobes or teeth can be short.
The distance between pinnae or pairs is meaningful.
Glumes can be narrow.
A fruit base can be cuneate. This is a base-shape statement.
A wall has a thickness. The examples are correct.
Margins and apices can be undulate.
A calyx can be bowl-shaped (crateriform).
'Spurred' means the corolla has a spur. That is a part (has-part spur), not a spur-shaped corolla. This is a wrong reading of the PATO term.
Membranes or the endostome can be transparent or hyaline.
Wood can be soft.
The examples only name the inflorescence type. The thyrse is the bearer, so 'present' on a thyrse adds nothing. The part is being read as the quality.
Stigmas can be fimbriate.
Apices can be acute or acuminate.
A staminal column can be glabrous.
Achenes can be hispid.
'Optical quality' is too generic. The examples are colours and should map to colour or to colour value terms.
